reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: The adenoids are a mass of lymphoid tissue at the back of the nasopharynx that normally enlarge in early childhood and regress toward puberty
Hypertrophy commonly causes nasal obstruction, mouth breathing, snoring and a characteristic hyponasal (blocked) voice
Long-standing obstruction and mouth breathing can produce the adenoid facies, with an open mouth, pinched nose, high-arched palate and dull expression
By blocking the Eustachian tube openings the adenoids predispose to recurrent otitis media and persistent middle ear effusion with conductive hearing loss
They also contribute to recurrent or chronic rhinosinusitis and postnasal discharge
Sleep-disordered breathing, ranging from snoring to obstructive sleep apnoea, is an important consequence and can affect growth and behaviour
Assessment uses history, examination, and either nasal endoscopy or a lateral nasopharyngeal radiograph to gauge the size of the adenoid pad
Adenoidectomy, often combined with grommet insertion or tonsillectomy, is indicated for significant obstruction, sleep apnoea or recurrent middle ear disease not responding to conservative measures
reference.pathophysiology: The adenoid (nasopharyngeal tonsil) is part of Waldeyer's ring and undergoes physiological enlargement with repeated exposure to inhaled and ingested antigens in childhood. Recurrent infection and allergy drive lymphoid hyperplasia so the pad enlarges enough to obstruct the posterior nasal choanae and the nasopharyngeal openings of the Eustachian tubes. Choanal obstruction forces mouth breathing and impairs sinus drainage, while Eustachian tube dysfunction interferes with middle ear ventilation, favouring effusion and recurrent otitis media. Chronic mouth breathing during the years of facial growth alters craniofacial and dental development, and narrowing of the upper airway during sleep produces snoring and obstructive sleep apnoea. The adenoid tissue can also act as a reservoir of infection and biofilm.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic rhinosinusitis with or without polyps
Deviated nasal septum or turbinate hypertrophy
Choanal atresia (particularly if present from birth)
Nasopharyngeal mass such as an angiofibroma in adolescent males
Foreign body in the nose (unilateral obstruction)
Nasopharyngeal tumour in adults with apparent adenoid tissue
additionalInvestigations: Nasal endoscopy to visualise and grade the adenoid pad
Lateral soft tissue radiograph of the nasopharynx to estimate adenoid size
Tympanometry and audiometry to detect middle ear effusion and conductive loss
Sleep assessment or polysomnography where obstructive sleep apnoea is suspected
Allergy assessment when an allergic component is likely
redFlags: Features of obstructive sleep apnoea such as witnessed apnoeas, restless sleep and daytime effects, which need timely evaluation
Strictly unilateral nasal obstruction or bloody discharge suggesting a mass or foreign body rather than adenoids
In an adolescent boy, profuse epistaxis with a nasopharyngeal mass suggesting juvenile angiofibroma
Apparent adenoid enlargement in an adult, which is unusual and should prompt exclusion of a nasopharyngeal tumour
Failure to thrive or significant growth and behavioural disturbance from chronic obstruction
reference.prognosis: Adenoid tissue tends to regress naturally with age, so many children improve over time, and adenoidectomy gives prompt and lasting relief of obstruction, sleep-disordered breathing and associated ear disease in those who need surgery.
pitfalls: Assuming any nasopharyngeal fullness in an adult is benign adenoid tissue and missing a tumour
Overlooking obstructive sleep apnoea and its effect on growth and behaviour
Attributing nasal obstruction solely to adenoids while missing allergy, septal deviation or a foreign body
Failing to assess and treat coexisting middle ear effusion and hearing loss
Neglecting the possibility of juvenile angiofibroma in an adolescent boy with obstruction and bleeding
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Refer for adenoidectomy when there is significant nasal obstruction, obstructive sleep apnoea or recurrent otitis media, as this gives prompt and lasting relief
Treat an allergic component with intranasal corticosteroid, saline irrigation and an antihistamine, which may reduce obstruction and defer surgery
Treat associated bacterial rhinosinusitis and recurrent infection with appropriate antibiotics
Insert ventilation tubes for persistent middle ear effusion with conductive hearing loss, often at the time of adenoidectomy
Adopt watchful waiting for milder cases, since adenoid tissue naturally regresses toward puberty
Monitor with tympanometry and audiometry, and assess sleep, growth and behaviour where obstruction is significant
Arrange sleep assessment or polysomnography and ENT referral when obstructive sleep apnoea is suspected
